sections.title: Recommending without giving orders
sections.content: In notices, emails and official advice nobody says *Haz esto*. You recommend. You know impersonal *se* from B1 Unit 6, *convendría* from B1 Unit 4, the conditional for advice from A2 Unit 26 and the imperfect subjunctive from B1 Unit 4. Put them together and you get the polite formulas of everyday B2: *se* + verb + *que* + subjunctive, or the conditional + *que* + imperfect subjunctive.

sections.title: Two ways to recommend
rows: Se recomienda que los visitantes lleguen temprano.
Sería conveniente que habláramos con la jefa.

sections.title: Why the conditional?
sections.content: The conditional makes the advice softer and more polite. Compare *Es conveniente que revisen el aviso* (direct) with *Sería conveniente que revisaran el aviso* (polite). With the conditional, the verb after *que* is always in the imperfect subjunctive.

items.spanish: Se recomienda que los visitantes lean el aviso antes de entrar.
items.english: Visitors are recommended to read the notice before entering.

items.spanish: Se sugiere que cada persona traiga su propia botella de agua.
items.english: Each person is advised to bring their own bottle of water.

items.spanish: Sería conveniente que usted hablara con la jefa hoy.
items.english: It would be advisable for you to speak to the boss today.

items.spanish: Convendría que revisáramos la sugerencia antes de la reunión.
items.english: It would be a good idea for us to check the suggestion before the meeting.

sections.content: To name the people you are advising, add *a* + group: *Se recomienda a los visitantes que lleguen temprano*. To advise in general, with no one in particular, use an infinitive: *Se recomienda llegar temprano*.
